title: Wayfinding is not signage — Image Wiki
text:
Wayfinding is not signage
  Signage is the objects on the wall. Wayfinding is a stranger actually arriving. You can add signs and make wayfinding worse.

  
    Termwayfinding vs signage
    Also calledsignage, wayfinding system, orientation
    Not the same assign legibility, map design, branding of a building
    Read8 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Information belongs at the choicesLegible London's two good ideasCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Think about the last time you were properly lost in a building. There were signs. Probably a lot of them. You stood at a junction reading one that said the same thing as the last four, and it did not tell you which of the two corridors in front of you led to the place you wanted.
That is the distinction. Signage is a set of objects: plates, posts, arrows, maps. Wayfinding is an outcome — a person who does not know the place ends up where they meant to go, without stopping, doubling back, or asking. The objects are only instruments, and adding more of them can make the outcome worse.
Central London is the proof. When Transport for London had the problem studied, the consultancy AIG counted at least 32 separate pedestrian wayfinding systems inside the Congestion Charging Zone alone, with inconsistent destination names, inconsistent distances, and no common standard for where a sign goes. Despite hundreds of maps and thousands of signs, one in seven Londoners had trouble finding their way on foot and around a quarter worried about getting lost. Signage was abundant. Wayfinding was broken.
Information belongs at the choices
The unit of wayfinding is not the sign, it is the decision point: a place where the route branches and the walker must pick. SEGD puts it flatly — every turning point is a decision, and the job is to give people information at each one. Between decisions, a walker needs nothing; they are already going the right way.

youward 614 signs, one messageyouward 6choosechooseconfirmarrive4 signs, four different jobsSigns by the metrerepeat the same thing between the junctionsSigns at the decision pointsone at each choice, one after the turn, one at the door

The same route to the same ward, and the only difference is where the signs are.
Left, fourteen signs repeating one message along the straights. The two junctions — the only places a mistake is possible — are no better served than the corridor walls, and the volume trains people to stop reading.
Right, four signs doing four different jobs: choose at each junction, confirm just after the second turn, arrive at the door. Legible London found the same thing in its pre-prototype testing: a reduced provision of signs could be just as effective if placed thoughtfully. The West End prototype put 19 new signs in and took 46 existing objects out.


Three consequences follow, and TfL's Interchange Signs Standard is built on all three.
Progressive disclosure. Give just enough information, just when it is needed — the phrase is Legible London's. TfL's sign sequence for a station is a clean example: overhead signs in the ticket hall name the primary services only; platform numbers and directions appear at the decision point between services, not before; line diagrams on the wall wait there for anyone who wants more detail.
Confirmation after the commitment. Having made the turn, the walker needs to know they were right. The standard requires that on reaching the platform a customer can see a sign confirming the platform number and direction. This is the sign type people forget to specify and the one that stops the anxious doubling-back.
Recovery. Wrong turns happen, so the system has to be forgiving. Where a platform has exits serving different lines, TfL requires clear direction to the far exit where the two routes divide — the choice is signed where it is made, not after. Legible London's own success criterion was whether people felt confident enough to get lost, knowing they could find their way back.
One more thing worth knowing: signs are the fallback, not the first resort. People navigate by architecture first — form, layout, size, light, a visible landmark — and turn to signage only when the building fails to explain itself. Which is also the order to look in when you audit a place.



Photo: Tom Page, Legible London sign, Villiers Street, 2025, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.
One object, three layers, top to bottom. The yellow cap and walking figure are a brand beacon — you learn once that yellow-plus-walker means pedestrian information here, and you can then spot it at 50 metres without reading anything. Under it, the area name answers "where am I": STRAND, with Embankment station below. Then the directional panel, which is the decision-point information: River Thames and South Bank ahead, Westminster and the Houses of Parliament right, Victoria Embankment Gardens left.
The bottom two-thirds is the map panel, here reduced to "New map coming soon" — a fair reminder that a wayfinding system is a maintenance commitment, not a construction project.


Legible London's two good ideas
Both of its most interesting decisions move work off the reader and onto the sign.
Heads-up maps. A map fixed to a post can be oriented to the environment, so it is drawn to match the direction you are facing rather than putting north at the top. That removes a mental rotation — a real operation with a real cost, and one that people are unevenly good at. The system still carries a north marker on every map and on the sign bases, because heads-up only works if you can also recover true north when you need it.

churchcafeyoufacingNthe cafe is to the right and belowNorth-uptop of the map is north; you rotate it in your headchurchcafeyoufacingNthe cafe is ahead and to the rightHeads-uptop of the map is where you are facing

The same three streets, the same café, the same you — the only change is which direction the top of the map represents.
Left, north-up: the café that is physically ahead and to your right sits to the right and below your dot, and the church that is on your left is drawn above you. To use it you must rotate the whole picture in your head. Right, heads-up: forward is up. Ahead is ahead, right is right, and the church appears on the left where you can see it. Nothing was simplified; the work was just done by the cartographer instead of the reader.


Time instead of distance. Legible London expresses scale in walking minutes, because research showed that is what people use when deciding whether to walk. "400 metres" needs converting before it answers your actual question, which is whether you will make your two o'clock. Five minutes is also a real unit of city structure — roughly 400 m, roughly the size of an identifiable London neighbourhood — so the maps come in two scales, a 15-minute planner and a 5-minute finder.
The reframing changes behaviour. 109 journeys between central London Tube stations are quicker on foot than underground; from Covent Garden, nine of the ten adjacent stations are. Nobody learns that from a distance in metres, and the Tube map actively hides it.



Photo: Robskedgell, Wayfinding monolith map in Stoke-on-Trent, 2023, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0. Cropped.
The Legible London pattern, exported to a different city — the same yellow cap and walker, the same area-name-then-destinations order. The panel headed "Walking from here" is the point: every destination is priced in minutes, not metres, and the list is ordered so you can scan for something that fits the time you have. Below it sit the two map scales, the wider planner above the local finder.


Common mistakes

"People are lost, so we need more signs." Count the decision points first. Usually the junctions are unsigned and the corridors are over-signed — and sometimes the existing signs are simply too small to read, which is arithmetic, not placement.
"The sign system is finished." Names change, departments move, panels get vandalised or emptied. An unmaintained sign that contradicts the building is worse than no sign, because it costs trust in every other sign.
"Each department can design its own." That is how a city ends up with 32 systems. Consistency is what lets a stranger learn the rules once.
"North at the top is correct." It is a convention, useful for planning and for anything you might rotate. For a fixed panel on a street it imposes work with no benefit.


Auditing a route in five minutes

Walk it as a stranger and mark every point where you could plausibly go two ways. Those are the decision points.
At each one, is the answer visible before you commit — not around the corner, not behind a departure board?
After each turn, is there anything confirming you were right?
Count the signs on the straights that repeat what you already know. That is your clutter budget.
If you deliberately go wrong, how many metres until something tells you so?
